report.tagline: A fan maker whose BLDC motor fans use about half the electricity of normal fans, now growing into smart locks and kitchen appliances.
report.simpleSummary: Most ceiling fans in India use old motors that waste power. Atomberg, started by two IIT Bombay graduates, makes fans with a better motor (called BLDC) that use around 28 to 35 watts instead of 70 to 80. They cost more upfront, about ₹3,000 to ₹6,000, but save money on electricity bills. Atomberg now sells about half of all premium fans in India, and also sells smart locks, mixer grinders and water purifiers.

overview.whatItDoes: Atomberg Technologies designs and makes energy-efficient BLDC ceiling fans with remotes and smart controls. It started in 2012 and sold motors and fans online first, then built a dealer network. It now also sells smart door locks, mixer grinders, water purifiers and juicers, and sells its own motors and controllers to other businesses.
howItWorks: Atomberg designs its own BLDC motors and electronics in-house.
Fans are made at its factories and partner plants.
Sales happen on Amazon, Flipkart, its website and through electrical shops and dealers.
Electricians install the fan; Atomberg's app or remote controls speed and modes.
After-sales service is handled by Atomberg's service network.
Its motor technology is reused in mixers and sold as components to other firms.
overview.valueProposition: Pay a little more for a fan once and save on electricity every month. A fan running 12 hours a day can save around ₹1,000 to ₹1,500 a year on the bill, so it pays back in 2 to 3 years.

painPoints.pain: Kitchen mixers are loud and weak.
painPoints.howSolved: BLDC mixers with more power and less noise.

businessModel.summary: Atomberg makes money by selling fans and appliances at a premium price over regular fans. Fans earn strong profit; kitchen appliances and component sales are still losing money.
businessModel.pricing: Fans mostly ₹2,500 to ₹6,000 on its website and marketplaces; smart locks and mixers priced separately.
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a ₹3,500 fan. Making it might cost ₹2,000 (product margin was about 43%). Dealer or marketplace fees, shipping and service take ₹700 to ₹900. Marketing takes about ₹350. That leaves around ₹300 to ₹400 per fan. Losses in newer categories eat up this profit at the company level. These per-unit numbers are estimates.

howTheyGetUsers: Government energy rating rules pushing efficient fans
whatBringsUsersBack: Other appliances under the same brand
growth.moat: Own motor and electronics technology and design skill. It took years to make cheap, reliable BLDC fans. Big brands now make BLDC fans too, so the moat is narrowing to brand and R&D speed.

northStar.metric: Units of electricity saved per month by Atomberg fans in use
northStar.why: Shows real customer value: lower bills. It grows with fans sold and fans that keep working.

strengths: Clear product edge in energy savings
weaknesses: Service network thinner than big brands

improvementIdeas.idea: Built-in surge protection on all fans
Show yearly savings tracker in app
Focus kitchen products on one hit item first

pmLessons: A real product improvement can beat big brands if it saves customers money.
Explain value in rupees saved, not technical terms.
Expanding into new categories can drain profits.
Incumbents will copy, so keep improving.
